chunks.text: Four ninety-nine isn't five dollars. But your brain thinks it's four.
We read prices left to right, and the first digit wins.
So four ninety-nine feels like four. Five feels like five.
One cent cheaper. But in your head? A whole dollar.
In one famous catalog test, the same dress was sold for thirty-four, thirty-nine and forty-four dollars.
The thirty-nine dollar dress sold best. Even better than the cheaper one!
Why? A nine at the end can whisper: deal.
So where did ninety-nine start? Nobody knows for sure.
One popular story: owners wanted cashiers to open the register and make change, so they couldn't pocket the cash.
Ninety-nine cent prices were in newspaper ads by eighteen-eighty.
Some fancy places do the opposite. Round prices. No nines. Nothing that says bargain.
Some even drop the dollar sign completely. That's part two.
So next time you see a nine, ask yourself: is it a deal, or just a nine?
